text: Open-angle glaucoma is frequently treated first with a top- ical beta blocker or, increasingly, a prostaglandin ana- logue. It may be necessary to combine these drugs or add others such as a topical alpha2-adrenoceptor agonist or a The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed 1874 Miotics Mydriatics and Antiglaucoma Drugs topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor to control intra-ocular pressure. Miotics are usually reserved for third-line use. It has been suggested that each type of drug should be tried alone first before resorting to combination therapy. If further reduction of intra-ocular pressure is required a systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor may be used but long-term treatment is poorly tolerated. If this is unsuc- cessful, surgery (trabeculectomy) or laser treatment (trabeculoplasty) is usually indicated. Laser treatment ap- pears to be as effective as topical drug therapy23 although its effects may be short-lived.24 It has been suggested that it might be of use in the initial treatment of older patients who cannot use eye drops or when surgery needs to be postponed or is contra-indicated.1 Some also recommend that laser treatment is tried before a miotic or an oral car- bonic anhydrase inhibitor, because of the potential adverse effects associated with these drugs.5 Early studies in the UK suggested that surgery was superior to drug or laser treatment in reducing intra-ocular pressure and preserving vision;24 however, a later study25 showed no difference in the progression of visual field loss in patients with newly diagnosed glaucoma after the initial use of surgery or drug treatment. A recent systematic review has also found that in early mild open-angle glaucoma progression of the dis- ease over 5 years was no different if first treatment was with medication or trabeculectomy but trabeculectomy was associated with more eye discomfort, an increased risk of cataract, and reduction in visual acuity.26 The early use of surgery was often advocated in Europe, especially in younger patients, although it is now rarely used as the primary form of treatment, even in the UK.4 It is essential to start treatment for an acute attack of angle- closure glaucoma within 24 to 48 hours. If treatment is de- layed adhesions may form between the iris and the cornea (peripheral anterior synechiae) and the trabecular mesh- work may be damaged. Chronic angle-closure glaucoma may then develop with permanently raised intra-ocular pressure which ultimately leads to total loss of vision (ab- solute glaucoma). The initial treatment aims to produce a rapid reduction in intra-ocular pressure. A miotic such as pilocarpine is used topically to constrict the pupil while a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor such as acetazolamide is giv- en orally or by intravenous injection.
